newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-MATTHAEUS WOULD LIKE TO END CAREER IN U.S.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MATTHAEUS WOULD LIKE TO END CAREER IN U.S.

text.p: Bayern Munich captain Lothar Matthaeus, Germany's most capped international, would like to end his playing career with a year in the United States and then move into management.

"I like the American mentality very much and I could also learn English there for a career as a manager or as some kind of representative," the 35-year-old said in a newspaper interview published on Tuesday.

Matthaeus's contract at Bayern runs until 1998 and he has not yet said if he plans to stay beyond then. He said he would particularly love to play on the U.S. West Coast, mentioning Los Angeles as a possible location.
Matthaeus also said his feud with Bayern team mate Juergen Klinsmann, whom he had accused of plotting to keep him out of the national team, was over.
"I never hated him," he said in the interview with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily. "I simply didn't trust him. I had the impression he was playing little games behind my back which were damaging me."
But he added: "When I offer to shake someone's hand after a certain period of time, that means it's all forgotten. That's what Juergen and I did."
Matthaeus said he would not be interested in becoming a coach but would like a management role such as former Germany striker Rudi Voeller now had at Bayer Leverkusen.
The former World Cup-winning captain said any management job would not have to be at Bayern and suggested he might like to work in Switzerland, where his wife and son live.

Matthaeus said the highly public row with Klinsmann had made him more cautious about what he told the press. But he could not resist a snipe at his colleagues when asked why Bayern had played unattractive soccer in the first half of the season.
"They say a lot of players came back tired from the European championships. I personally don't think that's a valid reason," he said.
"The players had three weeks' holiday. I played in seven major tournaments, never had three weeks' holiday and was still in good form afterwards."
